title: The servant who argues
hook: a servant who serves while arguing proudly loses the master's favor (Asa di Var M2, ang 474)

segments.voice: Yesterday, speak sweetly, and your line: sweet words, sweet life. Who heard your warm words? Today Guru Angad pictures someone who does the work, but can't stop talking back. Day five hundred fifty-nine.

You ask someone at home to take out the trash. They do it. Eventually. But first there's a sigh, then a speech about how they always do everything, then a list of what you haven't done, then the bag dragged slowly to the door. The trash gets taken out. Technically, the job is done. And somehow nobody in the house feels better. Guru Angad, the second Guru, wrote a short salok about exactly this kind of service, the kind that gets done with an argument attached.
screen: `THE TRASH, EVENTUALLY.` → `A SIGH, A SPEECH, A LIST.` → `THE JOB DONE, NOBODY BETTER.`

segments.voice: The salok is marked mahala 2, Guru Angad's, on ang 474. In paraphrase: a servant who works for a master, but serves with pride and argues, who talks a great deal, doesn't win the master's pleasure. Then the other picture. One who loses the self and serves gains some honor. And the last line: Nanak, the one who clings to the Master meets the Master; that clinging is accepted. Notice what the arguing servant does right. He shows up. He does the work. The salok doesn't say he's lazy. The problem is everything he wraps around the work: gaarab, pride, and vaad, argument. Endless talk about how hard it is, how unfair, how much better he'd do it if he were in charge. The work gets done, but the service doesn't arrive, because service isn't only an action. It's a way of offering it. Remember the contented servants on day five hundred forty-five. That pauri was Guru Nanak's. This salok is his successor's, and it shows the shadow side of the same picture. The contented served, and were accepted. The proud served too, and argued, and lost the favor. There's a story Sikhs tell about Guru Angad himself, when he was still called Bhai Lehna. Guru Nanak asked for hard and dirty jobs to be done, and while others objected, Lehna simply did them. Tradition holds that's part of why Guru Nanak chose him. Whatever the details, the salok reads like it came from someone who had lived it: serving without the speech.
screen: `PRIDE AND ARGUMENT AROUND THE WORK.` · `THE JOB DONE, THE SERVICE NOT.` · `LOSE THE SELF, GAIN HONOR.` · `BHAI LEHNA SIMPLY DID IT.` · then, large: `SERVE WITHOUT ARGUMENT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: serve without grumbling. Sit and breathe slowly. Think of one task waiting for you today that you'd normally do with a sigh: a chore, a request from someone, an errand. Picture yourself doing it all the way through without the commentary. No sigh. No list. No speech in your head. Just the work, offered. Notice whether something in you resists. Let it, and breathe. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you picture finishing. The bell holds the time.
Gaarab, pride: in Guru Angad's salok, one who serves with gaarab and argument doesn't please the Master; one who loses the self in service gains honor.
Your line: serve without argument. Today, do the task you pictured, and leave out the sigh and the speech entirely. Day five hundred fifty-nine.

screen: `DAY 559 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: HOW EACH PAURI SUMS UP.`

howItsDone: Sikhs hear Guru Angad's salok on the arguing servant in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and Sikh seva is meant to be done humbly, without complaint or display.

fork.setup: you're Bhai Lehna, and Guru Nanak asks for a hard, dirty job to be done. others object. what do you do?
options: explain why someone else should do it.
do it, and remind everyone afterward.
fork.reveal: tradition holds that Lehna simply did what was asked, and that this is part of why Guru Nanak chose him as the second Guru.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't argue with your boss.
what it means: work done with pride and complaint wrapped around it isn't service; losing the self in it is.
what a scholar hears: 'chaakar lagai chaakaree naale gaarab vaad'; the salok is Guru Angad's, and Sikh tradition remembers him as the servant who didn't argue.

sources.ref: Asa di Var, salok M2 (chaakar lagai chaakaree), Ang 474

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): cut a hook line that told the listener about their own life ('we've all been on both sides').

The salok is paraphrased; confirm 'chaakar lagai chaakaree naale gaarab vaad / galaa kare ghanereeaa khasam na paae saad / aap gavaa-e sevaa kare taa kichh paa-e maan / Nanak jis no lagaa tis milai lagaa so parvaan' and ang 474.

The Bhai Lehna stories (e.g. carrying a muddy bundle of grass, retrieving a bowl from a ditch) are kept general as 'hard and dirty jobs'; confirm the tradition's framing and that others' objections are fairly described.
